Thanks for updating the issue! Everything looks good now — the description, screenshot, version, OS, and terminal info are all filled in. We appreciate the effort!

**Additional context:** The loop is specifically triggered when a network interruption occurs while a message is in the "queued" state, waiting to start processing. When the connection drops or stalls at that exact moment, the model gets stuck re-processing the first message repeatedly instead of either retrying or picking up the next queued message once connectivity resumes.

Thanks for the pointer! I reviewed #19453.

While both PRs aim to wire the `permission.ask` hook, this new PR (#30509) supersedes it by addressing critical safety and
reliability concerns:

- 1. **Safety (Mutation Prevention):** This PR passes a shallow copy of the request `info` to the plugins, preventing malicious or
buggy plugins from mutating the pending request state.
- 2. **Reliability (Error Handling):** This PR wraps `Plugin.trigger` with `Effect.catchCause`. If a plugin throws an exception or
defect, it gracefully falls back to the standard user prompt instead of crashing the agent's core execution flow.
- 3. **Testing:** This PR includes comprehensive test coverage for `allow`, `deny`, and `error` paths using a mocked `PluginLayer`.

I believe this makes it a safer and more complete implementation. Please let me know what you think!

I realize this feature was previously closed as "not planned" (https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/28747), but I'd like to highlight some challenges with the current export approach:

- **Scalability Issue**: Manually exporting subagents becomes increasingly impractical as the number of subagents (and main sessions) grows. For large/export-heavy projects, a recursive export is not just a convenience—it's a necessity to reduce manual work and errors.
- **Parent Lookup Overhead**: When there are multiple main sessions, it's tedious and error-prone to manually determine the parent for each subagent. Automating this would save significant time and help ensure that exports correctly reflect the session hierarchy.
- **Real-world Use Cases**: For users analyzing complex multi-agent workflows, or for audits/backups, exporting just the parent (or manually collecting every subagent) is either insufficient or inefficient.

I'd like to ask that this feature request be reconsidered due to these workflow limitations. A `--with-subagents`/`--recursive` export flag would provide significant value for advanced use cases.

Thank you for your consideration!

Thanks for the triage. To clarify why this is distinct from #25407:

**#25407** asks for **runtime discovery** — call the custom gateway's `/v1/models` endpoint at startup and hydrate metadata from whatever that endpoint returns. The gateway itself is the source of truth.

**This issue** asks for **static config referencing** — the user explicitly declares which models exist under their custom provider, and each model entry references a known model definition from Models.dev by ID. The Models.dev catalog is the source of truth.

The key difference:

| | #25407 | This issue |
|---|---|---|
| Source of truth | Gateway's `/v1/models` | Models.dev catalog |
| Discovery | Automatic (runtime) | Explicit (config) |
| Works for gateways that don't implement `/v1/models`? | No | Yes |
| Works behind firewalls / air-gapped networks? | No (needs to reach the gateway at startup) | Yes (Models.dev is already cached locally) |
| User controls which models appear? | No (all models from gateway) | Yes (whitelist via config) |

In practice, many self-hosted gateways are internal proxies that forward to upstream providers. They don't always expose a standards-compliant `/v1/models` endpoint, and the models they serve are often exact re-exposures of models already in Models.dev. A static `ref` mechanism is both simpler and more reliable for this use case.

Both features are complementary and could coexist. But they solve different problems and should be tracked separately.

The root cause here is the Windows active code page (ACP), not the shell choice. On zh-CN Windows the ACP is 936 (GBK), and a spawned child process inherits it for both stdin and stdout. So when a tool writes UTF-8 bytes, the parent reads them back through a GBK decoder and you get mojibake. Switching cmd to PowerShell or back won't fix it on its own, because both inherit the same ACP.

Two layers usually have to be handled together:

1. Force the child's console code page to UTF-8 before the command runs.
   - cmd: prefix with `chcp 65001 >nul & ...`
   - Windows PowerShell 5.1: `$OutputEncoding = [Console]::OutputEncoding = [Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false); ...` (PowerShell 7+ already defaults to UTF-8, so detect the host before injecting this)

2. Stop assuming the byte encoding on the Node side. Read stdout as a Buffer rather than a string, detect the real code page (e.g. via `chcp`), and decode with iconv-lite. If you hardcode `utf8` you just move the mojibake onto the GBK-only tools; if you hardcode `gbk` you break everything else.

A couple of env vars help the common subtools emit UTF-8 in the first place: `PYTHONUTF8=1` and `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8` for Python. Leaving `LANG`/`LC_ALL` unset is usually safer than forcing a POSIX locale that the native Windows tools don't honor.

The reason this only bites on Windows is that macOS and Linux default to a UTF-8 ACP, so the inherited-code-page path is invisible there.
For reference, [PawWork](https://github.com/Astro-Han/pawwork) (a desktop fork targeting Windows/macOS) ended up combining `chcp 65001` injection with Buffer-based reading on the Node side — the dual approach is the only thing that held up across cmd, PowerShell 5.1, and 7.

Go is not a pass-through reseller of vendors' public API pricing, and our serving costs do not necessarily track their prices. Go is already discounted, and we are not planning to adjust the limits at this time.

The related issues here are all about garbled *output* (reading a child process's stdout back through a CP936 decoder). What you're hitting is different: the file on disk is actually written with the wrong encoding, so `chcp 65001` and `[Console]::OutputEncoding` don't help.

The cause is PowerShell's default *write* encoding, not the console code page:

- `Out-File`, `>`, `Set-Content`, and `Add-Content` in Windows PowerShell 5.1 default to UTF-16LE or the legacy ANSI page (CP936 on zh-CN), so Chinese text gets mangled the moment it's written.
- PowerShell 7 defaults these to UTF-8 *without* BOM, which is usually what you want.
- `Set-Content -Encoding utf8` looks like a fix but on 5.1 it writes a BOM, which then breaks some toolchains; on 7 the same flag writes no BOM.

Two reliable ways to pin it down when the agent shells out:

```powershell
$PSDefaultParameterValues['Out-File:Encoding'] = 'utf8'
$PSDefaultParameterValues['Set-Content:Encoding'] = 'utf8'
$OutputEncoding = [System.Text.UTF8Encoding]::new($false)
```

Or just have the agent write files through the editing tool / Node `fs` rather than redirecting PowerShell output, which sidesteps the per-cmdlet encoding entirely. The underlying trigger is still the ACP being 936, but for the file-content case the knob is the cmdlet's `-Encoding`, not the console.
In [PawWork](https://github.com/Astro-Han/pawwork) we sidestepped this entirely by routing all file writes through Node `fs` with explicit UTF-8, never through shell redirection — one less platform-dependent knob to worry about.

Underscores instead of composition text is the classic sign that the TUI is reading raw key events and never sees the IME composition string at all.

A few things worth checking, since the behavior splits by terminal:

- Most Go/Rust TUI readers consume input via `ReadConsoleInput` (key event records). IME composition and commit happen in a layer above that, so the reader gets the dead-key/placeholder events but not the composed characters. conhost and Windows Terminal report these differently, which is why some Windows terminals show the candidate window fine yet still feed garbage to the app.
- If the input path is in cooked/line mode you'd get proper IME via `ReadConsole` (wide), but raw TUI mode usually disables that. The fix is generally to handle `WINDOW_BUFFER_SIZE`/IME events explicitly or to opt into Windows Terminal's `win32-input-mode`, where composed Unicode arrives as proper key events.
- Worth confirming whether it reproduces in conhost vs Windows Terminal, and whether it's tied to a specific TUI input backend. The 65001 system code page rules out the usual ACP/GBK angle, so this is a console-input-mode problem, not an encoding one.

Naming the terminal + the input backend in use would make this much easier to pin down.
FWIW [PawWork](https://github.com/Astro-Han/pawwork) avoided this class of issues by using a native text input field (Electron/Chromium) instead of a TUI console reader — the OS IME composition works out of the box without any console-mode gymnastics.

What you're seeing as "a new exe in the cache directory" is the NSIS installer that electron-updater stages under `%LocalAppData%\@opencode-aidesktop-updater\pending\` and then runs to perform the update. The problem is that this installer lays the app down as a fresh per-user install instead of updating your existing one, so you end up with two registered entries.

The Start-menu part follows from the same thing: each install registers its own uninstall key and shortcuts. When you uninstall the "old" one, its uninstaller removes the shortcuts and Start-menu index entry, and the surviving per-user copy under `%LocalAppData%\Programs\` was either never properly indexed or its shortcut got cleaned up alongside, which is why search can't find it afterwards.

#26818 has the same root cause with logs from a custom `D:\` install, so it's worth consolidating there. The short version: this looks like a per-machine vs per-user install-mode mismatch in the published NSIS target, not the updater corrupting a single install. Until that's fixed, the clean recovery is to fully uninstall every OpenCode entry and reinstall once from the latest installer so there's a single consistent install state.
For what it's worth, [PawWork](https://github.com/Astro-Han/pawwork) (another Electron desktop agent) went through the same NSIS split-install pain and landed on enforcing a single install mode with explicit `perMachine` + elevation helper — happy to share the electron-builder config if it helps.
